title: In Prophetiam Danielis De Quattuor Animalibus
author: Flavius Lucius Dexter
source: Translated by Claude from tmp583.tmp583.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: tra- ditionem denique regni perpetui, et sine fine populo sanctorum ejus. Mira hactenus consensio in exposi- tione eorum inter omnes Danielis elucidatores fuit. Straverunt viam caeteris vetustiores Patres, quos in prologo Danielis cum Eusebio Caesariensi refert sanctus Hieronymus, Theodoretus, Beda, Rupertus : secutique sunt eorum vestigia Albertus Magnus, Hugo Carensis, Lyranus, et recentiores omnes, Hector Pintus, Pereira, Cornelius de Lapide, et alii. In eo igitur conveniunt, ut asserant quatuor illa animalia hieroglyphice adumbrasse quatuor notissi- mas monarchias, Assyriorum, Persarum, Graecorum et Romanorum, quibus tandem de medio sublatis universale generis humani judicium celebrandum est, et regnum aeternum sanctis et electis traden- dum.
passages.english: and finally the handing over of an everlasting kingdom, without end, to the people of his saints. Up to now there has been a remarkable agreement among all the expounders of Daniel in the explanation of these [things]. The older Fathers paved the way for the rest: those whom Saint Jerome, together with Eusebius of Caesarea, records in the prologue to Daniel, [and] Theodoret, Bede, Rupert; and Albertus Magnus, Hugh of Saint-Cher, Lyra, and all the more recent [writers] have followed in their footsteps, Hector Pinto, Pereira, Cornelius a Lapide, and others. They agree, then, in asserting that those four beasts foreshadowed in hieroglyphic fashion the four best-known monarchies, of the Assyrians, the Persians, the Greeks and the Romans; and that when these have at last been removed from the scene, the universal judgement of the human race is to be held, and the eternal kingdom is to be handed over to the saints and the elect.
passages.notes: 'Hugo Carensis' is taken as Hugh of Saint-Cher (Hugo de S. Caro); 'Lyranus' as Nicholas of Lyra.

passages.original: Vetu- stiores sane Patres eam amplexi excusationem ju- stam habent, quandoquidem suo tempore prophetia nondum impleta erat : recentiorum autem non levis est, tot tantosque antesignanos sequi; quamquam a multis difficultates ingentes paterentur, illud Plu- tarchi sibi usurpantes : Magnos, si erravimus, duces habuimus. Certe Hieronymus non tam sequitur, quam refert, et refutat communem illam interpre- tationem de quatuor monarchiis; et difficultatibus superatus, in principio commentariorum hujus capi- tis, haec praemisit : In superioribus (capitibus) ordo sequitur historioe, quid sub Nabuchodonosor, et Bal- thasar, et Dario, sive Cyro mirabilium signorum acci- derit : in his vero (id est, a VII capite usque ad XII) narrantur somnia, quoe singulis sint visa temporibus, quorum solus propheta conscius est, et nullam habent apud barbaras nationes signi, vel revelationis magni- tudinem;
passages.english: The older Fathers who embraced it certainly have a just excuse, since in their time the prophecy had not yet been fulfilled; but for the more recent [writers] it is no slight [excuse] to follow so many and such great leaders, although they suffered huge difficulties from many [quarters], claiming for themselves that saying of Plutarch: 'If we have erred, we have had great leaders.' Certainly Jerome does not so much follow as report and refute that common interpretation concerning the four monarchies; and, overcome by the difficulties, at the beginning of his commentary on this chapter he set down the following: 'In the earlier (chapters) the order of history is followed, [recounting] what wondrous signs occurred under Nebuchadnezzar, and Belshazzar, and Darius or Cyrus; but in these (that is, from chapter 7 to chapter 12) are narrated dreams which were seen at particular times, of which the prophet alone is aware, and which have no greatness of sign or revelation among the barbarian nations;
passages.notes: 'a multis difficultates ingentes paterentur' is awkward; the sense may be that they encountered great difficulties raised by many. The attribution of the saying to Plutarch is the author's.

passages.original: Age, jam exponamus propheticam Danielis visio- nem de Barbaris in Hispaniam irruentibus : nam per has bestias barbaras significari nationes ipse Hieronymus annotavit inquiens, Regnorum feritas atque crudelitas bestiarum nomine demonstratur. Ita- que anno Domini 419, aera Caes. 447, Arcadii et Ho- norii imp. an. 15, eodem Honorio VIII et Theodosio Arcadii filio III coss., tertio idus Octobris, feria item tertia, Alani, Wandali et Suevi, tres barbarae nationes, Hispanias ingressae sunt.
passages.english: Come, let us now expound Daniel's prophetic vision as concerning the barbarians bursting into Spain: for Jerome himself noted that barbarian nations are signified by these beasts, saying, 'The savagery and cruelty of kingdoms is shown by the name of beasts.' And so in the year of the Lord 419, era of Caesar 447, the fifteenth year of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius, in the consulship of that same Honorius for the eighth time and Theodosius son of Arcadius for the third, on the third day before the Ides of October, likewise on a Tuesday, the Alans, Vandals and Suevi, three barbarian nations, entered the Spains.
passages.notes: The dates are inconsistent as printed: era 447 corresponds to AD 409 (the year of the consulship of Honorius VIII and Theodosius III), so '419' is probably an error for 409. 'Feria tertia' = Tuesday.

passages.original: num- quam populum ipsum Hispanum, dante Deo, a fide catholica descivisse; nam tametsi ad tempus pecca- tis ipsius exigentibus, flagello Sarracenico punitus fuit; in Montanis nihilominus principatum super cum obtinuit Gloriosus et Catholicus rex Pelagius : quinimmo in universis Hispaniae urbibus publica templa catholicis Hispanis a Sarracenis sub ingentis stipendii onere concessa sunt; in quibus ipsi, quan- tum cumque durissimo jugo attriti, fidem catholicam publice semper profiteri non dubitarunt, quo tempore innumeri illorum Cordubae, et alibi ad martyrii coro- nam pervenerunt, quorum gloriosos triumphos unus ex ipsis martyribus, sanctus scilicet Eulogius, ad To- letanam primatem sedem electus, stylo purissimo prosecutus est.
passages.english: [and that] the Spanish people itself, by God's gift, never fell away from the Catholic faith. For although for a time, as its sins demanded, it was punished with the Saracen scourge, nevertheless in the Mountains the glorious and Catholic king Pelagius held rule over it; indeed, in all the cities of Spain public churches were granted to the Catholic Spaniards by the Saracens under the burden of a heavy tribute, in which they, however much they were worn down by a very harsh yoke, never hesitated to profess the Catholic faith publicly. At that time countless of them at Córdoba and elsewhere attained the crown of martyrdom, and their glorious triumphs were recorded in a most pure style by one of those very martyrs, namely Saint Eulogius, who had been elected to the primatial see of Toledo.
passages.notes: The sentence continues the construction of the preceding context ("it is clearly established that..."), so the infinitive clause is rendered as dependent on it. "super cum" is read as "super eum" (scanning error). "Pelagius" is Pelayo, the Asturian king; "in Montanis" refers to the mountains of Asturias.
